responses.strategic_rationale: Strategic rationale: The unit must reconcile high‑quality, longitudinal parasomnia data acquisition with limited budget, staffing, and participant burden. Core tensions involve balancing recruitment speed against inclusion rigor, staffing flexibility against annotation consistency, automation against human oversight, and expansion against data integrity. The selected levers target these conflicts by diversifying recruitment, optimizing shift patterns, streamlining annotation, developing event‑triage, adjusting compensation, and timing expansion. Together they aim to maximize event yield, maintain methodological rigor, and preserve financial sustainability while ensuring the facility’s scientific outputs meet publication and grant milestones.

levers.name: Recruitment Channel Diversification
levers.consequences: Increasing recruitment channels will raise enrollment speed, potentially exceeding the 30–35 participant target in year two, but may dilute pre‑screening quality, increasing the proportion of unproductive admissions and necessitating stricter exclusion verification.
options: Expand recruitment to include online sleep disorder forums and targeted social media ads to reach patients beyond local referrals.
Partner with regional sleep clinics to co-host educational webinars, positioning the unit as a trusted referral destination.
Implement a patient ambassador program where enrolled participants share experiences with peers, creating organic word‑of‑mouth referrals.
levers.review_lever: Broadening recruitment channels can accelerate enrollment but risks admitting participants who fail to meet strict inclusion criteria, potentially inflating the 20% unproductive admission threshold and triggering a costly external review.

levers.name: Staffing Shift Rotation
levers.consequences: A rotating shift model increases staff flexibility and reduces overtime, potentially lowering personnel costs, but may introduce variability in annotation consistency and increase training overhead for technicians transitioning between PSG and headband modalities.
options: Adopt a 12‑hour rotating shift schedule for technicians, ensuring continuous coverage while reducing overtime costs.
Introduce cross‑training for technicians in both PSG and headband monitoring to increase flexibility during peak event‑response periods.
Implement a staggered weekend rotation that pairs senior technicians with junior staff, fostering mentorship while maintaining night‑shift coverage.
levers.review_lever: Rotating shifts can cut overtime but may compromise annotation quality if technicians lack consistent exposure to the same monitoring modality, potentially inflating inter‑rater variability and delaying data processing.

levers.name: Annotation Workflow Optimization
levers.consequences: Optimizing annotation workflow can cut per‑event review time, accelerating data availability for analysis, but may increase reliance on technician judgment for initial markings, potentially raising inter‑rater variability if the triage criteria are not rigorously defined.
options: Deploy a real‑time annotation dashboard that flags potential events for technician triage, reducing manual review time.
Introduce a two‑tier annotation protocol where technicians first mark events, then senior reviewers confirm, streamlining workload distribution.
Integrate automated event‑detection scripts that pre‑label likely parasomnia episodes, allowing technicians to focus on verification rather than initial marking.
levers.review_lever: Streamlining annotation speeds up data processing but risks higher inter‑rater variability if technicians lack clear triage guidelines, potentially compromising the reliability of event counts used in phenotyping analyses.

levers.name: Event‑Triage Algorithm Development
levers.consequences: Developing an event‑triage algorithm can reduce manual review load, enabling faster data turnaround, but may introduce false positives that inflate annotation time and risk misclassifying benign movements as parasomnia, affecting downstream phenotyping accuracy.
options: Train a supervised machine‑learning model on annotated PSG data to predict parasomnia events from headband and sensor streams.
Leverage unsupervised clustering of multimodal sensor features to identify novel event signatures, reducing reliance on labeled data.
Implement a hybrid rule‑based filter that flags high‑probability events for human review, balancing automation with expert oversight.
levers.review_lever: An automated triage system cuts review time but may generate false positives, increasing technician workload and potentially skewing event frequency estimates if benign movements are misclassified as parasomnia.

levers.name: Compensation Structure
levers.consequences: Adjusting compensation can improve participant retention and event yield, but higher payouts increase budget strain and may attract individuals motivated by financial gain rather than clinical relevance, potentially biasing the sample.
options: Introduce a tiered compensation model that rewards longer stays with incremental bonuses, incentivizing participants to remain until multiple events are captured.
Offer flexible meal plans and local transport vouchers to reduce participant burden, potentially improving retention and data completeness.
Implement a pre‑admission credit system where participants receive a refundable deposit that is returned upon study completion, enhancing commitment.
levers.review_lever: Higher compensation may boost enrollment and event capture but risks inflating costs and attracting participants whose primary motivation is financial, potentially compromising the representativeness of the study cohort.

levers.name: Expansion Timing Decision
levers.consequences: Choosing expansion timing balances resource allocation against data quality; early expansion may strain staffing and increase false‑alarm rates, while delayed expansion preserves quality but limits participant throughput and delays publication timelines.
options: Delay suite expansion until the pilot cohort demonstrates a false‑alarm rate below 5%, ensuring data quality before scaling capacity.
Proceed with a phased expansion to 12 suites after achieving a 90% event‑capture success rate in the first 20 participants.
Implement a real‑time monitoring dashboard that flags capacity bottlenecks, allowing dynamic adjustment of suite utilization without full physical expansion.
levers.review_lever: Expanding suites early can boost enrollment but risks compromising data integrity if staffing and annotation pipelines are not fully mature, potentially leading to higher false‑alarm rates and delayed analyses.

responses.strategic_rationale: The residential parasomnia unit must balance limited capital, rigorous safety, and high-quality longitudinal data. Core tensions arise between recruitment speed and participant burden, staffing flexibility and event responsiveness, manual annotation labor and data fidelity, and budget rigidity versus adaptive resource allocation. The selected levers target these conflicts by redefining incentive structures to sustain enrollment, optimizing suite scheduling to capture rare events, automating annotation to reduce human error, adjusting ethics review cadence to accelerate protocol evolution, flexing funding to respond to emergent needs, and structuring interdisciplinary collaboration to integrate clinical insight with engineering solutions. Together, they create a resilient operational framework that preserves scientific rigor while enabling timely progress toward validation and phenotyping milestones.

levers.name: Participant Retention Incentive Design
levers.consequences: Adjusting the incentive structure can improve participant retention, potentially extending stay durations and data yield, but it also raises per-participant costs and may introduce bias if participants alter reporting to maximize compensation.
options: Offer tiered cash compensation tied to total nights, incentivizing longer stays but increasing per-participant cost.
Provide complimentary health consultations and sleep hygiene workshops, reducing monetary expense while fostering participant engagement.
Introduce a points-based reward system redeemable for local cultural experiences, engaging participants without direct cash outlay but requiring coordination with local partners.
levers.review_lever: While tiered cash compensation may boost retention, it risks inflating budget and could bias self-reporting of symptoms; non-monetary perks may not be equally motivating across demographics; the points system adds logistical complexity and may dilute focus on scientific outcomes.

levers.name: Suite Utilization Scheduling
levers.consequences: Reconfiguring suite scheduling can maximize occupancy and reduce idle time, yet it may limit the ability to rapidly respond to unexpected parasomnia events, potentially missing critical data.
options: Implement fixed nightly block scheduling, maximizing suite occupancy but limiting rapid response to flagged events.
Adopt a staggered shift model with overlapping nights, increasing responsiveness but complicating staffing coordination.
Introduce a dynamic booking algorithm that reallocates suites based on real-time event likelihood, optimizing utilization but requiring sophisticated monitoring.
levers.review_lever: Fixed nightly blocks streamline operations but may delay capture of sporadic events; staggered shifts enhance responsiveness yet strain staffing; dynamic allocation optimizes use but adds algorithmic complexity and potential scheduling conflicts.

levers.name: Data Annotation Workflow Automation
levers.consequences: Automating annotation reduces manual labor and speeds data processing, but reliance on imperfect algorithms can introduce systematic errors that compromise event validity and downstream analyses.
options: Deploy semi-automated event detection using machine learning to pre-label events, reducing scorer time but requiring periodic human review.
Introduce rule-based threshold alerts for abnormal sensor patterns, speeding annotation but risking false positives.
Implement a hybrid crowdsourcing platform where trained volunteers assist in preliminary labeling, lowering costs but raising consistency concerns.
levers.review_lever: Semi-automated detection cuts scorer workload but depends on model accuracy; rule-based alerts may flood with false positives, burdening reviewers; volunteer crowdsourcing reduces cost yet may compromise labeling quality and data integrity.

levers.name: Ethics Compliance Cadence
levers.consequences: Altering the frequency of ethics reviews can accelerate protocol changes and recruitment, yet it may overwhelm oversight bodies and increase administrative burden, potentially compromising thoroughness.
options: Adopt quarterly ethics board reviews to accelerate protocol adjustments, expediting recruitment but increasing administrative load.
Maintain annual reviews to ensure thorough oversight, slowing changes but providing stability.
Implement a rolling review process with continuous monitoring, balancing agility and oversight but requiring additional compliance staff.
levers.review_lever: Quarterly reviews accelerate protocol changes but may overwhelm the board and staff; annual reviews offer stability but can delay necessary adaptations; rolling reviews provide balance yet demand extra compliance resources and may dilute board focus.

levers.name: Funding Allocation Flexibility
levers.consequences: Shifting budget allocations across years can provide resources for emergent needs, but it risks misaligning spending with milestone-driven deliverables and eroding contingency reserves.
options: Reallocate unused year-one funds to year-two equipment upgrades, accelerating capability but reducing contingency for unforeseen costs.
Maintain strict year-by-year budget lock, ensuring milestone alignment but limiting responsiveness to emerging needs.
Introduce a rolling reserve fund that can be tapped across years, providing flexibility but demanding rigorous monitoring.
levers.review_lever: Reallocating year-one funds accelerates upgrades but erodes safety net for later contingencies; strict yearly locks preserve milestone focus but hinder rapid response; a rolling reserve offers flexibility yet demands vigilant oversight to prevent misallocation.

levers.name: Interdisciplinary Collaboration Structure
levers.consequences: Redesigning collaboration mechanisms can enhance integration of clinical and technical expertise, yet it may create role ambiguity and increase coordination overhead, potentially slowing decision cycles.
options: Establish a joint steering committee with representatives from neurology, engineering, and psychology, fostering cross-disciplinary input but potentially slowing decision-making.
Create dedicated liaison roles that bridge clinical and technical teams, improving communication but adding personnel costs.
Implement a shared digital workspace for real-time data sharing and discussion, enhancing transparency but requiring secure infrastructure.
levers.review_lever: A joint steering committee promotes integration but may create decision bottlenecks; liaison roles improve communication yet increase staffing costs; a shared workspace boosts transparency but demands robust security and may expose sensitive data.

system_prompt:
You are an expert strategic analyst. Generate solution space parameters following these directives:

1. **Output Requirements**
   - You must generate 5 to 7 levers per response.
   - Each lever's `options` field must contain exactly 3 qualitative strategic choices as plain strings.

2. **Lever Quality Standards**
   - Consequences: describe the direct effect of pulling this lever, then at least one downstream implication or trade-off. Be concise and grounded — only cite numbers the project context provides directly. Target length: 30–60 words.
   - Options MUST:
     • Represent genuinely distinct strategic pathways (not just labels)
     • Include at least one unconventional or non-obvious approach
     • NO prefixes (e.g., "Option A:", "Choice 1:")

3. **Strategic Framing**
   - Name each lever using language drawn directly from the project's own domain — avoid formulaic patterns or repeated prefixes
   - Frame options as complete strategic approaches
   - Ensure levers challenge core project assumptions

4. **Validation Protocols**
   - For `review_lever`:
     A one-sentence critical review (20–40 words). Examples:
     - "Switching from seasonal contract labor to year-round employees stabilizes harvest quality, but the idle-wage burden during the 5-month off-season adds a fixed cost that erases the per-unit savings unless utilization reaches year-round levels."
     - "Each additional clinical site requires its own IRB approval, site-initiation visit, and staff credentialing — a sequential overhead that compounds rather than parallelizes, so doubling site count does not halve enrollment time."
     - "Pooling catastrophe risk across three coastal regions reduces expected annual loss on paper, but a single regional hurricane season can correlate all three simultaneously, turning the diversification assumption into a concentration risk at the worst possible moment."
     Do not use square brackets or placeholder text.

5. **Prohibitions**
   - NO prefixes/labels in options (e.g., "Option A:", "Choice 1:")
   - NO generic option labels (e.g., "Optimize X", "Tolerate Y")
   - NO placeholder consequences or bracket-wrapped templates
   - NO fabricated statistics or percentages without evidence from the project context
   - NO marketing language (e.g., "game-changing", "cutting-edge", "revolutionary")

6. **Length Limits**
   - Keep each `review_lever` to 20–40 words.
   - Each option: 15–25 words, a concrete actionable approach with an action verb.
   - Maintain parallel grammatical structure across options
   - Ensure options are self-contained descriptions
user_prompt:
File 'plan.txt':
Plan:
Establish a 3-year residential longitudinal research unit in Bonn, Germany, for the study of adult NREM parasomnias — sleepwalking, confusional arousals, and sleep terrors — with a secondary exploratory arm for REM sleep behavior disorder under a separate protocol with dedicated neurologic screening, reflecting RBD's distinct clinical trajectory per current AASM guidance. The facility is affiliated with University Hospital Bonn's Department of Epileptology, leveraging its existing long-term video-EEG monitoring culture, and addresses a specific methodological gap: traditional single-night polysomnography rarely captures infrequent parasomnia events, while outpatient actigraphy lacks physiological resolution. The unit houses 8 active sleep suites at launch in a converted residential property in a quiet Bonn neighborhood, renovated for safety (padded corridor edges, restricted-opening windows, silent exterior door alarms, fire safety, acoustic treatment, network cabling, accessibility modifications) while preserving a domestic feel — if the environment is too clinical, naturalistic behavior is suppressed. Physical capacity exists for 12 suites, but expansion is deferred until the pilot proves acceptable data quality, manageable false alarm rates, safe staffing ratios, and usable annotation throughput. Sensing uses a tiered acquisition model: nightly low-burden monitoring via dry-electrode EEG headbands, contact-free mattress sensors, unobtrusively mounted infrared cameras, ambient microphones, and environmental sensors; scheduled enhanced nights with fuller PSG montage including standard scalp EEG, EOG, chin EMG, and leg EMG on the first night, one mid-stay night, and the final night per participant; and escalation nights deploying full PSG after technician-flagged events to capture recurrence at clinical-grade resolution. All streams are time-synchronized and stored in EEG-BIDS-compatible format on a local NAS with nightly encrypted backup to university storage, annotated in real time by the night technician and later scored by two independent raters using AASM criteria with inter-rater reliability reported. Public data sharing is limited to de-identified physiological and sensor data under data use agreements — bedroom video carries severe privacy constraints and is not deposited in public repositories. The scientific program has three explicit aims: Aim 1, establish and operationally validate the residential capture model as safe, ethics-approved, and sustainable; Aim 2, characterize within-person and between-person parasomnia patterns longitudinally, including episode frequency, morphology, triggers, and temporal clustering; Aim 3, develop and benchmark semi-automated event-triage tools that rank probable parasomnia episodes and reduce manual review burden, evaluated against dual human scorer agreement rather than promising autonomous diagnosis.

Participant recruitment targets adults aged 18–65 with NREM parasomnia confirmed through a structured pre-admission pathway: specialist clinical interview, collateral history from bed partner or household member where available, prior or screening polysomnography, and a structured exclusion checklist adjudicated by the PI. Explicit exclusions are nocturnal epilepsy or suspected epilepsy mimics, untreated obstructive sleep apnea, active major substance use disorder, severe psychiatric instability, and wandering or injury risk beyond facility capability. Recruitment channels are the University Hospital Bonn sleep clinic, regional neurologist referrals, and the Deutsche Gesellschaft für Schlafforschung und Schlafmedizin network, with per-night compensation of €80 plus meals. A matched control group provides baseline nocturnal movement, arousal patterns, and false-positive sensor activity under identical residential monitoring conditions, enabling benchmarking of the event-triage tools against normal nocturnal behavior. Event-yield planning assumes that based on the inclusion criterion of at least 2 self-reported episodes per month, approximately 70–80% of admitted participants will produce at least one captured and adjudicated event during a 2–8 week stay; stays may be extended up to 2 additional weeks for participants with zero captured events after the initial period, capped at 10 weeks total, with a protocol ceiling of 20% unproductive admissions before triggering a recruitment-criteria review. The core team is 9 people: a PI who is a board-certified sleep medicine physician, 2 postdoctoral researchers in sleep neurophysiology and computational neuroscience respectively, 3 research technicians rotating night shifts to ensure safe coverage of 8 active suites with adequate margin for event response and annotation, a clinical psychologist specializing in sleep disorders, a data engineer managing the sensor pipeline, and a study coordinator handling recruitment, consent, scheduling, and ethics compliance.

Budget is €3.8 million over 3 years, gated: €1.8M year one covering property lease and renovation at approximately €750K, equipment at approximately €450K, staff hiring accounting for German social insurance contributions and actual overnight coverage, ethics approval, and a pilot cohort of 15–20 participants; €1.2M year two covering full operations with 30–35 participants, the enhanced-night PSG program, first publications, and event-triage algorithm development; €800K year three conditional on demonstrable progress by month 24. Personnel costs are approximately €2M over three years and remaining funds cover participant compensation, independent scoring time, data storage and retention, regulatory and legal work, and contingency. Funding sources are DFG research grant and University of Bonn internal research funding as the primary pillars, with a pharmaceutical industry partnership as optional upside rather than a feasibility requirement — if secured, the academic team retains full publication rights with the pharma partner receiving a 30-day pre-publication comment window only. Success criteria at 36 months: safe residential monitoring operations sustained for at least 24 months, enrollment of 50–70 NREM parasomnia participants plus matched controls, capture of a prespecified minimum number of independently adjudicated parasomnia events sufficient for Aim 2 phenotyping analysis, 2–3 peer-reviewed publications in sleep medicine journals covering methods validation and longitudinal characterization, a benchmarked semi-automated event-triage model with reported sensitivity, specificity, and agreement against dual human scoring, de-identified physiological dataset deposited in a recognized repository, and a submitted phase-two grant proposal for expansion and intervention studies. Failure triggers: if by month 18 the facility has enrolled fewer than 25 participants or captured fewer than 40 adjudicated events, the program undergoes external review. Governance is a 3-member external scientific advisory board reviewing progress every 6 months, with the PI holding operational authority and budget reallocations above €50K requiring board approval. Banned words: AI, blockchain, app, VR, AR, gamification, wearable startup, consumer product, DAO, NFT, metaverse, smart home, autonomous diagnosis, digital therapeutic, SaaS, marketplace, validated (in the context of claiming a mature deployable system). Pick a realistic scenario — this is an early-stage clinical research facility producing methods validation and phenotyping work, not a finished diagnostic platform.
